raw_text:
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has progressively moved from a last-resort therapy for inoperable aortic stenosis to a mainstream treatment across surgical-risk strata, aided by smaller delivery systems, CT-based planning, improved vascular closure, and standardized endpoint definitions [1-8]. Nevertheless, severe iliofemoral calcification, small vessel caliber, hostile aortoiliac tortuosity, prior vascular reconstruction, or extensive peripheral artery disease still preclude transfemoral arterial access in a clinically important minority of patients. Transcaval access was developed to preserve the procedural ergonomics of retrograde transfemoral TAVR while avoiding diseased iliofemoral arteries: a large-bore sheath is introduced from the femoral vein, advanced to the inferior vena cava (IVC), and deliberately passed into the adjacent infrarenal abdominal aorta [9-13].

The conceptual leap of transcaval access is that a controlled aortic and caval perforation need not produce catastrophic hemorrhage. Preclinical and early clinical work showed that in the confined retroperitoneal space, aortic blood preferentially returns through the low-pressure caval defect, producing a transient aortocaval fistula rather than free bleeding [9,10]. Procedurally, pre-procedural CT identifies a calcium-free right aortic wall target adjacent to the IVC, avoids interposed bowel or other structures, confirms adequate distance from renal arteries and the aortoiliac bifurcation, and anticipates a covered-stent bailout strategy [11,13]. Under fluoroscopy, an electrified 0.014-inch guidewire is directed from the IVC toward an aortic snare, exchanged for a stiff wire, and used to deliver a conventional TAVR sheath. After valve implantation, the tract is closed, traditionally with off-label nitinol occluders such as Amplatzer duct or muscular ventricular septal defect devices [12-16].

The evidence base remains observational but is unusually systematic for an alternative-access technique. The initial 19-patient human experience established feasibility in patients otherwise ineligible for standard TAVR access [10]. In the prospective NHLBI transcaval TAVR study, access was successful in nearly all attempted cases and enabled TAVR in patients considered poor candidates for transfemoral or transthoracic access; however, bleeding, transfusion, and vascular complications reflected the extreme risk of the population and the limitations of permeable, non-dedicated closure devices [14]. One-year follow-up was reassuring: most aortocaval fistulas spontaneously closed, there were no late major transcaval vascular complications, and fistula patency was not associated with worse survival or heart-failure hospitalization [15]. A purpose-built transcaval closure device subsequently demonstrated promising preclinical and early human results, including more complete immediate hemostasis, but it has not yet become widely available [16].

Transcaval access is also part of the broader field of transcatheter electrosurgery [17]. Compared with surgical transapical or direct-aortic approaches, it avoids thoracotomy, pleural violation, and myocardial puncture. Compared with transaxillary/subclavian access, it avoids manipulation of the aortic arch from an upper-extremity route and may reduce embolic stroke in selected patients. In a contemporary propensity-weighted comparison from experienced centers, transcaval and transaxillary TAVR had similar bleeding and vascular outcomes, but stroke or transient ischemic attack was less frequent after transcaval access [21]. Single-center comparative data similarly suggest shorter hospitalization and less kidney injury than other alternative routes, although selection bias is unavoidable [20]. Recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses report high procedural success, approximately 6% to 7% 30-day mortality in selected nontransfemoral populations, and complication rates broadly comparable to other extrathoracic alternative-access approaches [23,24].

Patient selection is critical. Favorable candidates have prohibitive iliofemoral arterial anatomy but an infrarenal aorta that offers a noncalcified target adjacent to the IVC, without interposed bowel, major lumbar vessels, dissection, intramural hematoma, or extensive thrombus. Relative concerns include severe right-sided heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension, or marked tricuspid regurgitation, because even a temporary left-to-right shunt may be poorly tolerated [13]. Coagulopathy and inability to reverse anticoagulation can compromise closure. Operators should prepare for aortic balloon tamponade, covered-stent implantation, device retrieval, and re-crossing of the tract; best-practice reviews emphasize proctorship, CT-fluoroscopy correlation, and disciplined closure technique [13,22].

Although most experience is in TAVR, transcaval access has been adapted for other large-bore structural and endovascular interventions. Reports describe use through prosthetic or grafted abdominal aortas, sheathless techniques, redo transcaval TAVR, left-sided venous access, and facilitated crossing in hostile calcified anatomy [12,26-29]. Outside valve intervention, transcaval access can deliver large mechanical circulatory support devices while avoiding limb ischemia in cardiogenic shock, and early series of transcaval Impella delivery support feasibility in carefully selected patients [19,30]. These applications reinforce the central attraction of the technique: it converts a large-bore arterial access problem into a venous access and controlled-closure problem.

In contemporary practice, transcaval access should be viewed neither as experimental improvisation nor as a universal replacement for transfemoral TAVR. It is a specialized, CT-planned, electrosurgical alternative for patients with no safe iliofemoral arterial route and for centers prepared for its unique closure and bailout requirements. Wider adoption will depend on training, prospective comparisons against transcarotid and transaxillary approaches, and commercial availability of dedicated closure systems. For structural heart programs treating increasingly complex peripheral vascular disease, transcaval access remains an important technique in the alternative-access armamentarium.
